claims.text: Sintering Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co at 900–1000 °C triggers precipitation of a continuous nanoscale Ti/V-rich BCC intermetallic network at grain boundaries.
The Ti/V-rich grain-boundary network acts as a diffusion barrier that suppresses Mg volatilization.
The Ti/V-rich network acts as a hardening phase.
Sintering below 800 °C fails to nucleate the network because atomic mobility is insufficient.
Sintering above 1000 °C causes Mg loss that disrupts continuity of the refractory-rich network.
The ball-milled Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co starting powder is a metastable BCC solid solution.
The ball-milled powder has a high defect density.
Milling may produce surface oxide layers on the powder.
SPS in the 800–1000 °C range, with emphasis on 900–1000 °C, can maximize diffusion while avoiding excessive Mg loss.
An SPS pressure of approximately 30–50 MPa is suitable for the proposed processing.
A short SPS dwell of approximately 10–15 minutes limits Mg evaporation.
Above 800 °C, diffusion becomes sufficiently active for Ti and V to segregate from the supersaturated BCC matrix and form a secondary-phase network.
The secondary-phase network retards inward oxygen diffusion and promotes formation of a protective passive film.
The precipitates enhance hardness by impeding dislocation motion.
Optimized SPS will produce a bulk density greater than 95% of theoretical density.
Optimized SPS will produce a Vickers hardness greater than 400 HV.
The optimized material will have lower oxidation and corrosion rates than material sintered below 800 °C or above 1000 °C.
Mg depletion above approximately 1000 °C destabilizes the BCC matrix and yields a porous, brittle microstructure with poor corrosion resistance.
Competing Mg-Al or Mg-Fe intermetallics may form instead of the proposed Ti/V-rich barrier phase.
Parabolic oxidation kinetics indicate diffusion-controlled oxidation, whereas linear kinetics indicate surface-reaction-controlled oxidation.
